whoIsThisFor.heading: Who should take the MuleSoft Hyperautomation Developer exam?

personas.label: Automation developers
personas.description: You build workflows across APIs, robotic process automation, and no-code integration tools.

personas.label: MuleSoft developers expanding into RPA
personas.description: You build integrations and want to apply bots to processes that still depend on a user interface.

personas.label: Salesforce automation specialists
personas.description: You use Flow and want to extend automation across enterprise systems with MuleSoft tools.

examDifficulty.heading: How challenging is the MuleSoft Hyperautomation Developer exam?
examDifficulty.summary: The exam spans several automation tools rather than testing only one development skill. You need to choose between APIs, RPA, Composer, and Salesforce Flow for different parts of a process.
bullets: 60 scored questions in 90 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
70% to pass, which is 42 correct answers out of 60.
Tool selection: Know when an API, RPA bot, Composer flow, or Salesforce Flow fits the task.
RPA concepts: Review how bots are built, managed, triggered, and secured.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Practice mapping a business process across tools. Use APIs when a suitable interface exists, RPA for UI-only tasks, and human approval steps where judgment is required. Aim for at least 80% on practice questions.

examFormat.heading: MuleSoft Hyperautomation Developer exam format
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online or in person. Questions cover automation design across MuleSoft and Salesforce tools.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Some questions describe a multi-step business process and ask which automation tool should handle each step or how the tools should be coordinated.
bestWayToPass: Choose the right tool: Use APIs where systems provide an interface, RPA for suitable UI-only tasks, Composer for supported no-code cloud connections, and Flow for Salesforce process logic.
Review RPA operations: Understand bot building, orchestration, attended and unattended modes, and credential handling.
Plan human review: Use a human-in-the-loop step when a decision or approval is required.
Design for exceptions: Check existing records, handle failures, and measure completion and exception rates.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers building end-to-end automation solutions that combine MuleSoft APIs, RPA bots, Composer, and Salesforce Flow to automate complex business processes across multiple systems.

blocks.heading: Designing a Hyperautomation Solution
blocks.body: Hyperautomation combines automation technologies across an end-to-end process. MuleSoft APIs connect systems with available interfaces. RPA bots can handle selected tasks that depend on user interface interaction. Composer supports no-code integrations between supported services, while Salesforce Flow automates processes within Salesforce. Use the most reliable interface available for each step and coordinate tools through a clear process design.

blocks.heading: MuleSoft RPA Builder and Manager
blocks.body: RPA Builder is used to create and edit bots that automate user interface tasks. RPA Manager supports orchestration and monitoring of bot processes. Attended bots work alongside a person; unattended bots run without a person actively guiding each step. Secure credentials through approved credential management and limit access. A UI bot can be sensitive to screen changes, so prefer stable elements and design for error detection.

blocks.heading: Composer, APIs, and Flow
blocks.body: Composer lets business users configure supported cloud-to-cloud integrations without writing a Mule application. Mule APIs are suited to systems with a supported interface and can provide reusable access to data or actions. Salesforce Flow automates Salesforce processes, including decisions and user interactions. Choose based on system support, transformation needs, reliability, and the skill required to maintain the solution.

blocks.heading: Document Processing and Human Review
blocks.body: Document processing can extract structured data from documents such as invoices and forms. Extraction results may need validation before they are used in a business process. Add a human review step when confidence is low or an approval is required. Do not assume every document or exception can be handled without human judgment.

blocks.heading: Orchestration, Exceptions, and Measurement
blocks.body: Orchestration sequences automations and coordinates data and outcomes across them. Plan what should happen when a record already exists, a system is unavailable, or a step fails. Record the failure, retry safely when appropriate, and resume or alert a person rather than reporting false success. Measure completion, exceptions, time saved, and results against the manual baseline.

scenarioTips.h2: How to prepare for the MuleSoft Hyperautomation Developer exam
scenarioTips.intro: Break a scenario into steps and select the tool that best fits each one. Consider whether an API exists, whether a person must interact, and how exceptions will be handled.

blocks.heading: Choose APIs Before UI Automation
blocks.body: Use an API when the target system provides a suitable interface. Consider RPA when the required interaction is available only through a user interface.

blocks.heading: Know Attended and Unattended Bots
blocks.body: Attended bots work alongside a person; unattended bots run independently according to the process design. Consider how each mode affects scheduling and credentials.

blocks.heading: Add Human Review Where Needed
blocks.body: Use an approval or review step when the process requires judgment, policy approval, or validation of uncertain document data.

blocks.heading: Handle Errors and Duplicates
blocks.body: Check whether a record already exists and define the next action. Log failures and resume or alert rather than repeating steps blindly.

blocks.heading: Measure Business Results
blocks.body: Track completion rates, exceptions, processing time, and business outcomes. Compare the results with the process before automation.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Related credentials for hyperautomation developers
nextCertsAfter.intro: Build on automation skills with a MuleSoft integration or Salesforce developer credential.

sampleQuestions.question: A legacy application has no API and can only be operated through its desktop interface. Which tool may fit?
options: A Platform Event that reports each screen change
MuleSoft RPA
An HTTP connector pointed at the application URL
A database connector reading its internal store
sampleQuestions.explanation: RPA can automate suitable tasks through a user interface when the application has no usable API.
whyWrong: A Platform Event can signal changes but cannot operate a desktop-only interface.
RPA is suited to automating an application through its user interface.
An HTTP connector requires an API or web endpoint the legacy app does not provide.

sampleQuestions.question: A business user wants to connect two supported cloud services without writing code. Which tool fits?
options: A DataWeave script run manually
An Anypoint Studio project built by a developer
A scheduled Apex class
MuleSoft Composer
sampleQuestions.explanation: Composer provides a no-code way to connect supported cloud services.
whyWrong: A manual DataWeave script does not give the business user a configured no-code flow.
Anypoint Studio requires developer work rather than no-code configuration.
A scheduled Apex class requires code and is not the Composer option.

sampleQuestions.question: What distinguishes attended and unattended RPA?
options: How the bot is licensed
Attended bots work with a person; unattended bots run independently
Attended bots run only in the cloud
Attended bots process structured data while unattended bots handle documents
sampleQuestions.explanation: Attended bots work alongside a user; unattended bots run without active user interaction.
whyWrong: Licensing is not the defining difference between attended and unattended bots.
Attended bots work with a person; unattended bots run independently.
Cloud versus desktop location is not the defining distinction.

sampleQuestions.question: An RPA bot breaks whenever a target application window shifts slightly. What design improvement can make it more robust?
options: Use stable element identifiers
Capture a screenshot after each action for later review
Increase every wait time
Run the bot more often to find failures sooner
sampleQuestions.explanation: Stable element identifiers are less sensitive to layout changes than fixed screen coordinates.
whyWrong: Stable element identifiers are less likely to shift when the screen layout changes.
Screenshots support troubleshooting but do not fix fragile element selection.
Waiting longer cannot correct selectors tied to screen coordinates.

sampleQuestions.question: What is document processing used for in an automation workflow?
options: Archiving completed documents only
Converting every document to one file format
Applying electronic signatures to all forms
Extract invoice and form fields
sampleQuestions.explanation: Document processing can extract fields from invoices and forms so later steps can use the structured data.
whyWrong: Archiving is not data extraction from a document.
Converting file formats does not extract business fields.
Electronic signing is separate from reading information in a document.

sampleQuestions.question: A business process must pause until a manager approves a value. What should the automation include?
options: A second process the manager starts manually
A fixed long delay before continuing
A human-in-the-loop approval step
An email notice while the process continues immediately
sampleQuestions.explanation: A human-in-the-loop step pauses the process until the required person reviews or approves the value.
whyWrong: A separate manual process can lose connection with the workflow state.
A fixed delay does not know whether approval has happened.
Human review is required before the automation continues.

sampleQuestions.question: Why expose an RPA process through an API?
options: To remove all RPA licensing requirements
Other systems can trigger it
To prevent the bot from using a user interface
To guarantee the target screen will never change
sampleQuestions.explanation: An API can make the RPA capability callable by other systems through a consistent interface.
whyWrong: RPA licensing still applies when its capability is called through an API.
An API provides a standard way for other systems to trigger the process.
The bot may still interact with the UI to complete the legacy task.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a risk of automating a process that is already broken?
options: Licenses always increase with each process error
The automation refuses to run until documentation is complete
It scales the existing bad outcome
RPA cannot handle any process with exceptions
sampleQuestions.explanation: Automating a flawed process can repeat and scale the existing problem unless the process is corrected first.
whyWrong: Licensing does not automatically scale with each process error.
Documentation alone does not correct a flawed process.
Automation can handle some exceptions, but a flawed process can still scale bad outcomes.

sampleQuestions.question: A bot may find that a target record already exists. What should the design do?
options: Check for the record and define a path for each result
Assume it will not exist and review errors weekly
Delete any duplicates after creating a record
Retry creation repeatedly until it succeeds
sampleQuestions.explanation: An explicit check and defined outcomes prevent duplicate creation and make the process predictable.
whyWrong: Checking for an existing record prevents duplicate creation and supports defined outcomes.
Ignoring the existing-record case can cause failures or duplicates.
Deleting records after creation can remove valid data.

sampleQuestions.question: What does orchestration add to individual automations?
options: It converts each automation into an API specification
It coordinates steps as one process
It reduces licensing costs automatically
It guarantees every step will always succeed
sampleQuestions.explanation: Orchestration coordinates the order and outcomes of multiple automation steps.
whyWrong: An API specification defines an interface, not the coordinated workflow.
Orchestration sequences and coordinates the steps.
License costs depend on product and usage, not orchestration alone.

sampleQuestions.question: A process runs overnight and fails at step seven of ten. What should the solution do?
options: Record failure, then resume or alert
Wait indefinitely without notifying anyone
Skip the last steps and report success
Restart from the beginning automatically every night
sampleQuestions.explanation: The workflow should record the failure and either resume safely or alert someone to resolve it.
whyWrong: Record the failure and resume safely or alert an operator.
An indefinite wait leaves the process stalled without visibility.
Skipping required steps and reporting success hides the failure.

sampleQuestions.question: Why must RPA credentials be handled carefully?
options: Credentials should be written into the process definition
Bots cannot use any multi-factor authentication
Each bot needs a separate license for every system
Bots sign in to systems as a user
sampleQuestions.explanation: RPA bots may authenticate as user accounts, so credentials and permissions need careful protection.
whyWrong: Credentials should use a secure store rather than be embedded in process definitions.
MFA support depends on the target system and design.
Bot licensing is not the reason credential handling requires care.

sampleQuestions.question: Which process is a sensible early automation candidate?
options: A yearly task done by one specialist
The most complex process in the organization
Repetitive work with stable rules
A process that changes its rules frequently
sampleQuestions.explanation: Frequent, repetitive work with stable rules is often a good place to start assessing automation.
whyWrong: A once-a-year task may not justify the investment for an initial pilot.
The most complex process is often a risky first automation.
Frequent, repetitive work with stable rules is a reasonable candidate.

sampleQuestions.question: How should a team measure whether an automation is working?
options: Count how many steps it performs
Count the volume of logs
Compare results with the manual baseline
Count how many systems it touches
sampleQuestions.explanation: Completion rates and exceptions compared with the baseline show whether the automation improves the process.
whyWrong: Step count does not show whether the business process improved.
Log volume alone does not measure business success.
Compare completion and exception rates with the manual baseline.

sampleQuestions.question: Which statement best describes hyperautomation?
options: Combining APIs, RPA, and people where each fits the process
Moving every automation into one Mule application
Replacing all integrations with RPA bots
Automating only tasks that require no code
sampleQuestions.explanation: Hyperautomation combines technologies and human work as needed across an end-to-end process.
whyWrong: This describes combining technologies and people to automate an end-to-end process.
One Mule application may not be the right fit for every process step.
RPA complements APIs rather than replacing every integration.
